An element has one `onclick`. Assigning to it silently replaces the handler that other code put there. `addEventListener()` adds a handler next to the others, and takes options such as `once` and `signal`.

Any assignment to a property named `on` plus a DOM event is reported, whatever the object is.

## Examples

Reported:

{/* bad {"count": 2} */}
```js
button.onclick = () => save(form);

window.onload = null;
```

Not reported:

{/* good */}
```js
const onClick = () => save(form);
button.addEventListener("click", onClick);

button.removeEventListener("click", onClick);
```

Reading the property is fine, and so is a name that is not a DOM event:

{/* good */}
```js
if (button.onclick) {
  button.click();
}

player.onscore = update;
```

## When not to use it

Objects that are not event targets can have a property such as `onmessage` or `onerror` as their only way to take a handler. Turn the rule off for the files that use them.
